title: Frequency Compensation
intro: Compensation reshapes the loop gain so that the phase margin is adequate.

blocks.text: Place a dominant pole far below all others, so the gain falls through 0 dB at -90 degrees phase, before the second pole contributes much. The price is lower bandwidth. For a single-stage op amp the load capacitor does this job automatically; the bandwidth is gm1/(2*pi*CL).
Miller compensation of two-stage op amps

A capacitor CC from the output of the second stage back to the first stage's output uses the Miller effect to put a large capacitance at the first stage's output, which pushes the first pole down. It also pushes the second pole up (this is called pole splitting):

blocks.source:
p1  =  1 / [ gm6 * R1 * R2 * CC ]       (dominant)
p2  =  gm6 / CL                         (approximately)
GBW =  gm1 / CC
z   =  gm6 / CC                         (right half plane)

items: The RHP zero adds phase lag; it is at gm6/CC, which is only a few times above GBW if gm6 is not much larger than gm1.
Put a resistor RZ in series with CC. With RZ = 1/gm6 the zero moves to infinity; with RZ larger it moves into the left half plane where it adds phase lead and can cancel p2.
The second pole at gm6/CL calls for gm6 well above gm1 (about 2 to 4 times) for 60 degrees phase margin.

blocks.text: In large-signal operation the first stage sources ISS into CC, so SR = ISS/CC. This limit is independent of the second stage unless the second stage cannot supply (CC + CL)*SR.

blocks.title: Compensating a two-stage amp
blocks.text: gm1 = 1 mS and CC = 1 pF. Find GBW. The second stage has gm6 = 4 mS and CL = 2 pF. Estimate p2 and the phase margin (ignoring the zero).
blocks.answer: GBW = 159 MHz, p2 = 318 MHz, PM about 63 degrees.

blocks.title: The RHP zero
blocks.text: In the amp above, where is the RHP zero? Is it important?
solution: z = gm6/(2*pi*CC) = 4e-3 / (2*pi * 1e-12) = 637 MHz, four times GBW.
A zero at 4x the unity-gain frequency adds arctan(1/4) = 14 degrees of phase lag, which would lower the phase margin to about 49 degrees; a nulling resistor RZ = 1/gm6 = 250 ohm removes it.
blocks.answer: z = 637 MHz; costs about 14 degrees of phase unless nulled with RZ = 250 ohm.
